text: CS101 CS101 — Algorithms & Data Structures Instructor: Dr. Maya Lindqvist Term: Autumn 2026 Credits: 7.5 ECTS This course is a first look at how to reason about running time, and how to pick a data structure without guessing. We start with asymptotic analysis, move through sorting and trees, and finish with graphs. You will write small programs, but the point is not typing. The point is being able to say *why* an algorithm is fast enough, and what happens when the input doubles. What you will be able to do Read a loop and give a tight big-O bound. Implement and compare insertion sort, mergesort, and quicksort. Use stacks, queues, hash tables, and binary heaps as tools rather than trivia. Run BFS, DFS, and Dijkstra on a weighted graph and explain the difference. Bring a laptop to the lab sessions. Pair work is allowed on the assignment unless a brief says otherwise. on Tuesday. Labs on Thursday. Readings are short on purpose; do them before the lab or the exercises will feel like a riddle. Office hours: Wednesday 13:00–14:30, room 4.12. CS101 Lecture: Sorting algorithms Week 3. We need a shared vocabulary before the assignment. A sorting algorithm takes n comparable items and permutes them into non-decreasing order. The interesting questions are: how many comparisons, how much extra memory, and whether equal keys keep their original order (stability). Insertion sort Walk left to right. For each item, slide it left until it sits in the already-sorted prefix. Best case: already sorted, Θ(n) comparisons. Worst case: reverse sorted, Θ(n²). In-place. Stable if you insert after equals, not before. Use it for tiny arrays, or as the base case of a recursive sort once the slice is under ~32 elements. A lot of “slow” sorts win on cache at that size. Mergesort Split the array in half, sort each half, merge the two sorted runs. Recurrence T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + Θ(n) → Θ(n log n) always. Needs Θ(n) extra memory for the merge buffer.

Stable, which is why it is the default when you care about a secondary key. The merge step is the whole idea: two pointers, copy the smaller head, drain the remainder. If you can write merge correctly you can write mergesort. Quicksort Pick a pivot, partition so smaller keys go left and larger go right, recurse. Average Θ(n log n). Worst case Θ(n²) if every pivot is an extreme. In-place (ignoring recursion). Not stable in the usual partition. Practical fix: median-of-three or random pivot, and fall back to insertion sort on small slices. Do not claim “quicksort is always faster than mergesort”. On objects with an expensive comparison, or when stability matters, mergesort is the grown-up default. What the assignment expects

You will visualise insertion sort and mergesort, not quicksort. That is deliberate: the two algorithms make opposite trade-offs (in-place vs guaranteed n log n), and the animation should make that visible. If a step does not move any bars, it is still a step. Count comparisons, not swaps, when you talk about cost in the write-up.

CS101 Assignment 1: Sorting visualiser Build a small visualiser that shows insertion sort and mergesort rearranging an array of bars. This is an individual-or-pair assignment. Pair work is allowed. Submit one repository and name both authors in the README. What to submit Source code that runs without undocumented steps. A 60-second screen recording of both algorithms on the same shuffled input. A short write-up (one page) comparing comparison counts on n = 20, 50, and 100. Submit before 23:59 on 14 October 2026. The portal timestamp is the one we use. Email is not a submission. Late work loses 10% per day. After three days we stop accepting it. Requirements 1. The user can generate a random array of n bars, n between 8 and 80. 2. Play, pause, and step-once controls. 3. Insertion sort and mergesort, selectable, sharing the same drawing code. 4. A counter of comparisons, updated live. You

do not need a framework. Canvas or SVG is enough. If you use a library, say why in the README. Grading Correctness of the two sorts is 50%. The animation being readable (not a blur of swaps) is 30%. The write-up is 20%. A visualiser that only works for n = 8 will not pass. Questions go in the course forum, not in the commit history.

CS101 Lecture: Graphs Week 6. From here on, the input is no longer a sequence. It is a set of vertices and a set of edges. Write G = (V, E). An undirected edge is a two-element set. A directed edge is an ordered pair. A weight is a number on an edge, usually a cost. Representations Adjacency list: for each vertex, the neighbours (and weights). Space Θ(V + E). This is the default. Adjacency matrix: a |V| × |V| table. Fine when the graph is dense, or when you need O(1) “is this edge present?”. If you store the matrix “because it is simpler” on a road network, you will run out of memory and also look like you skipped this slide. Walks you must know BFS from s discovers vertices in order of unweighted distance. Queue. Tree edges form a shortest-path tree in hops. DFS from s goes deep, then backtracks. Stack or recursion. Useful for cycle detection, topological sort, and connected components.

Dijkstra from s, non-negative weights: repeatedly settle the unsettled vertex with smallest distance. With a binary heap this is O((V + E) log V). Negative weights: do not use it; that is Bellman–Ford territory. A common exam trap: BFS is not Dijkstra with all weights equal *if you implement BFS on a weighted graph*. Equal weights plus Dijkstra is fine. BFS ignores the numbers. Project checkpoint (read this) The graph project is a shortest-path viewer over a campus map. You do not submit the full project this week. The graph project checkpoint is due 28 November 2026. Upload a working BFS and Dijkstra on the sample graph, plus a screenshot of one query. No write-up yet. If your Dijkstra disagrees with BFS on a unit-weight graph, fix that before you add fancy drawing. The drawing is the easy part.

DB201 DB201 — Introduction to Databases Instructor: Dr. Maya Lindqvist Term: Autumn 2026 Credits: 7.5 ECTS This course is about storing facts so that many people can ask questions without copying spreadsheets around. We start with entity-relationship modelling, then SQL, then normalisation so your schema does not fight you in week 8. You will use PostgreSQL in the labs. SQLite is acceptable for experiments on your laptop. Oracle is not required and will not be supported in office hours. Learning outcomes After the course you should be able to: Draw an ER diagram that a classmate can implement without guessing cardinalities. Write SELECT queries with joins, grouping, and nested subqueries. Translate a query into relational algebra and back. Put a messy table into 3NF and explain which anomaly you just removed. DB201 Lecture: Relational algebra and SQL SQL is the surface. Relational algebra is the reason the surface works. A relation is a set of tuples with named attributes. Operators take relations and return relations. If your query cannot be sketched with these operators, it is probably doing something procedural that belongs in the application. Core operators Select (σ) — keep rows that match a predicate. Project (π) — keep columns, drop duplicates in the algebra (SQL SELECT DISTINCT). Cross product (×) — every pair of rows. Rarely written by hand; joins are the grown-up form. Join (⋈) — a product plus a select, usually on a foreign key. Union, difference — same schema required. Aggregation — not in the original algebra; in SQL this is GROUP BY. When you write FROM a JOIN b ON a.id = b.a_id, you are doing a theta-join. When you forget the ON clause, you are doing a cross product and then

wondering why the result has 4 million rows. SELECT that we will actually use SELECT s.name, COUNT(*) AS n FROM enrolment e JOIN student s ON s.id = e.student_id WHERE e.year = 2026 GROUP BY s.name HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 ORDER BY n DESC; Read it in this order, not top to bottom: FROM/JOIN (the relations), WHERE (σ), GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT (π plus aggregates), ORDER BY (not relational). Subqueries belong in WHERE when you mean “exists a row”, and in FROM when you need a named intermediate relation. Correlated subqueries are allowed. They are also how people accidentally write O(n²) SQL. Integrity Primary keys, foreign keys, and NOT NULL are not bureaucracy. They are how the database refuses to store a fact that cannot be true. If your schema needs a comment “please do not
insert orphans”, you wanted a foreign key.

DB201 Lab 3: Writing queries This lab is formative. You still have to hand it in. Students who skip it tend to fail the midterm on joins. Work on the library schema from the lab zip. Do not invent your own tables; the autograder expects those names. Queries 1. List titles that have never been borrowed. 2. For each member, the number of loans in 2026, including members with zero. 3. The most borrowed ISBN in each category. 4. Members who borrowed a book that another member with the same postcode also borrowed, but not the same copy on the same day. Query 4 is the one that tells us whether you understood self-joins. A nested IN that returns the whole table is not a solution. Practicalities Submit a single lab3.sql file with the four statements in order, each ending with a semicolon. DB201 Assignment 1: ER modelling Design an ER diagram for a small public library, then write the relational mapping. Submit before 23:59 on 14 October 2026. PDF of the diagram plus a one-page mapping table. Pair work is not allowed for this brief. Domain Members borrow copies of books. A book has an ISBN, a title, and one or more authors. A copy has a barcode and a condition. A loan has a start date and a due date. Staff can also be members. Some members are children and must have a guardian who is an adult member. Fines accrue when a copy is returned after the due date. You do not need to model payments. What we mark Entity vs attribute choices (author is not a string on Book). Cardinalities that match the prose, including the guardian relationship. A clean mapping: keys, foreign keys, and junction tables where the diagram is many-to- many. No unexplained redundant attributes. A diagram
that looks pretty and cannot answer “can two copies share a barcode?” will not pass. Late work loses 10% per day. After three days the assignment is closed.

DB201 Week 6 lecture notes: Normalisation Normalisation is how we stop the same fact living in three rows so that an update hits only one of them. We will use a running example: a table LoanSheet(memberId, memberName, isbn, title, authorName, copyBarcode, loanedOn). That table is tempting. It is also a trap. 1NF Atomic values, no repeating groups. authorName as “Ng, Knuth” is already a 1NF problem if you ever want to query by one author. Split authors out. Repeating isbn1, isbn2, isbn3 columns is the other classic failure. 2NF Non-key attributes must depend on the *whole* key. If the key is (memberId, isbn) and memberName depends only on memberId, you are in 1NF but not 2NF. Pull member data into Member. 3NF Non-key attributes must not depend on other non-key attributes. title depends on isbn, not on the loan. Loan should hold copyBarcode and loanedOn. Copy points at Book. Book holds

title. After 3NF you should be able to change a title in one place and have every loan printout follow. BCNF is the extra step when a table has overlapping candidate keys. We will not examine BCNF in depth. If you can get to 3NF without losing a dependency, you are where this course needs you. Mini-project Take the denormalised events.csv on the course page (festival tickets, one row per sale). Produce 3NF relations, a short note of which anomalies disappeared, and the SQL CREATE TABLE statements. The normalisation mini-project is due 20 November 2026. Submit SQL plus a one-page PDF. This is individual work. If you only rename the wide table and call it 3NF, we will send it back. Show the functional dependencies.

Question 1 (2 points) Consider the function f (x) =    x2 − 4x x − 4 , x̸ = 4, a, x = 4. Determine the value of a for which f is continuous at x = 4. For x̸ = 4, x2 − 4x x − 4 = x(x − 4) x − 4 = x. Hence lim x→4 f (x) = lim x→4(x) = 4. (1 point) For continuity at x = 4 we need f (4) = limx→4 f (x), so a = 4. (1 point) Question 2 (3 points) Consider the function g(x) =    3x2 + b, x < 2, 6, x = 2, bx + 18, x > 2. Determine all values of b for which g is continuous at x = 2. For continuity at x = 2, we need lim x→2− g(x) = g(2) = lim x→2+ g(x). The left-hand limit is lim x→2−(3x2 + b) = 12 + b. (1 point) The right-hand limit is lim x→2+(bx + 18) = 2b + 18 (1 point) Since g(2) = 6, we need 12 + b = 6 and 2b + 18 = 6. Solving for b gives b = −6 in both cases. Therefore, b = −6. (1 point) 2/9

Question 3 (4 points) Consider the function h(x) = sin(2x)esin(2x) Find h′(x) Use the product rule h(x) = f (x)g(x) with f (x) = sin(2x), g(x) = esin(2x) Using the chain rule, f ′(x) = 2 cos(2x) (1 point) For g(x) we apply the chain rule twice, resulting in g′(x) = 2esin(2x) cos(2x) (2 points) Applying the product rule, we get: h′(x) = f ′(x)g(x) + f (x)g′(x) Thus, h′(x) = 2 cos(2x)esin(2x) + 2 sin(2x)esin(2x) cos(2x) = 2 cos(2x)esin(2x)(1 + sin(2x)) (1 point) 3/9

Question 4 (4 points) Given the function f (x) = 1 3 x3 + x2 − 8x − 5 Find the critical points of f , classify them using the first or second derivative test, and determine the interval where f is concave up and concave down. First compute f ′(x) = x2 + 2x − 8 = (x + 4)(x − 2). So the critical points are x = −4, x = 2. (1 point) The second derivative is f ′′(x) = 2x + 2. At x = −4, f ′′(−4) = −6 < 0, so f has a local maximum at x = −4. (1 point) At x = 2, f ′′(2) = 6 > 0, so f has a local minimum at x = 2. (1 point) For convexity, solve f ′′(x) = 2x + 2 = 0 =⇒ x = −1. Thus f ′′(x) < 0 when x < −1, so f is concave down on (−∞, −1). Also f ′′(x) > 0 when x > −1, so h is concave up on (−1, ∞). (1 point) 4/9

Question 5 (6 points) Compute ∫ 2 0 x2exdx We use integration by parts with u = x2, dv = exdx du = 2xdx, v = ex (1 point) Therefore, ∫ x2exdx = x2ex − 2 ∫ exxdx (1 point) Using integration by parts again on ∫ exxdx We get u = x, dv = exdx du = 1dx, v = ex (1 point) Thus, ∫ exxdx = xex − ∫ exdx = xex − ex (1 point) Substituting back ∫ x2exdx = x2ex − 2 ∫ exxdx = x2ex − 2(xex − ex) = ex(x2 − 2x + 2) + C (1 point) Now to find the definite integral ∫ 2 0 x2exdx = [ex(x2 − 2x + 2) + C]2 0 = e2(22 − 2 · 2 + 2) + C − (e0(0 − 0 + 2) + C) = 2e2 − 2 (1 point) 5/9

Question 6 (4 points) Evaluate ∫ 3x2 x3 + 1 dx We use substitution: u = x3 + 1 Thus du = 3x2dx (1 point) Therefore ∫ 3x2 x3 + 1 dx = ∫ 1 u du (1 point) Hence ∫ 3x2 x3 + 1 dx = ln |u| + C (1 point) Substituting back, ∫ 3x2 x3 + 1 dx = ln |x3 + 1| + C (1 point) 6/9

Question 7 (5 points) Construct the degree 3 Maclaurin polynomial of f (x) = sin 2x We first find the derivatives f ′(x) = 2 cos 2x f ′′(x) = −4 sin 2x f ′′′(x) = −8 cos 2x (3 points) Evaluate these at x = 0: f (0) = 0, f ′(0) = 2, f ′′(0) = 0, f ′′′(0) = −8 (1 point) The degree 3 Maclaurin polynomial takes the form P3(x) = f (0) + f ′(0)x + f ′′(0) 2! x2 + f ′′′(0) 3! x3. Therefore, P3(x) = 0 + 2x + 0 + −8 6 x3 = 2x + −4 3 x3. (1 point) 7/9

Question 8 (6 points) Solve the initial value problem y′ + 4y = e−3x, y(0) = 2 This is a first-order linear differential equation: y′ + 4y = e−3x. The integrating factor is μ(x) = e ∫ 4 dx = e4x. (1 point) Multiply both sides by e4x: e4xy′ + 4e4xy = ex. The left-hand side is d dx ( e4xy ) . (2 points) Thus d dx ( e4xy ) = ex. Integrating gives e4xy = ex + C. (1 point) Therefore, y = e−3x + Ce−4x. (1 point) Using y(0) = 2, 2 = 1 + C, so C = 1. Hence y = e−3x + e−4x. (1 point) 8/9

Question 9 (6 points) Find the maximum and minimum values of f (x, y) = −2x + 2y subject to the constraint x2 + y2 = 3. Let g(x, y) = x2 + y2 − 3. Then ∇f = (−2, 2), ∇g = (2x, 2y). (1 point) Using Lagrange multipliers, ∇f = λ∇g. So −2 = 2λx, 2 = 2λy, x2 + y2 = 3. (1 point) From the first two equations, x = − 1 λ , y = 1 λ . Therefore, y = −x. Substitute this into the constraint: x2 + (−x)2 = 3. So 2x2 = 3 =⇒ x = ± √ 3 2 . Since y = −x (y depends on x), we get the candidate points (√ 3 2 , − √ 3 2 ) , ( − √ 3 2 , √ 3 2 ) . (2 point) Now evaluate f on both candidate points and determine the maximum and minimum: f (√ 3 2 , − √ 3 2 ) = −2 √ 3 2 − 2 √ 3 2 = −4 √ 3 2 Also, f ( − √ 3 2 , √ 3 2 ) = 2 √ 3 2 + 2 √ 3 2 = 4 √ 3 2 Therefore, the maximum value is max f = 4 √ 3 2 , and the minimum value is min f = −4 √ 3 2 . (2 point) 9/9

Critical points of functions Critical points. A number c in the domain of f is called a critical number if f ′(c) = 0 or f ′(c) does not exist. The corresponding point (c, f (c)) is called a critical point on the graph. First derivative test. Suppose c is a critical number. - If f ′(x) changes from positive to negative at c, then f has a local maximum at c. - If f ′(x) changes from negative to positive at c, then f has a local minimum at c. - If the sign of f ′(x) does not change, then c is not a local extremum. c local max f ′ > 0 f ′ < 0 c local min f ′ < 0 f ′ > 0 3 / 8

Convexity and Concavity Concavity. For a twice differentiable function f : If f ′′(x) > 0 on an interval, then f is concave up (or convex) there. If f ′′(x) < 0 on an interval, then f is concave down there. A point where concavity changes is called an inflection point. Second derivative test. Suppose f ′(c) = 0. If f ′′(c) > 0, then f has a local minimum at c. If f ′′(c) < 0, then f has a local maximum at c. If f ′′(c) = 0, the test is inconclusive. concave up f ′′ > 0 concave down f ′′ < 0 4 / 8

Linear approximations If f is differentiable at x = a, then near a the graph of f is well approximated by its tangent line. The linear approximation (or linearization) of f at a is L(x) = f (a) + f ′(a)(x − a). Idea. For x close to a, f (x) ≈ L(x) = f (a) + f ′(a)(x − a). This is useful for quick estimates of values that are hard to compute exactly. x y a L(x) f (x) Visualization: https://www.desmos. com/calculator/jaecvccdpj?lang=nl 5 / 8

Taylor series If the Taylor polynomials of f centered at a continue indefinitely, we obtain the Taylor series ∞X n=0 f (n)(a) n! (x − a)n. When a = 0, this is the Maclaurin series. Interpretation. - A Taylor series gives an infinite polynomial representation of a function near its center. - In practice, we often use a partial sum to approximate the function. - If a function is analytic, it can be defined by its Taylor series with perfect precision (no error) 7 / 8

Key takeaways - Critical points come from f ′(x) = 0 or where f ′(x) does not exist. - The first derivative test classifies extrema via sign changes of f ′. - The second derivative describes concavity and helps classify critical points. - Linear approximations use tangent lines to estimate function values locally. - Taylor polynomials match derivatives at a center; Taylor series extend this idea to infinitely many terms. 8 / 8

Partial derivatives Differentiation can be extended from single-variable functions to multi-variable functions through partial differentiation: ∂ ∂x f (x, y) = lim h→0 f (x + h, y) − f (x, y) h (partial derivative of f w.r.t. x) ∂ ∂y f (x, y) = lim h→0 f (x, y + h) − f (x, y) h (partial derivative of f w.r.t. y) Intuition: vary one of the variables while keeping all other variables fixed. Critical points for multivariable functions For a differentiable function f (x, y), a point (a, b) is a critical point if ∂ ∂x f (a, b) = 0 and ∂ ∂y f (a, b) = 0. Equivalently, ∇f (a, b) = 0. Geometric meaning. When ∇f (a, b) = 0, the surface has no first-order change in either coordinate direction. So the tangent plane is horizontal, which implies: - a local minimum, - a local maximum, - or a saddle point. 3 / 8

Second derivative test for multivariable functions For a twice differentiable function f (x, y), the matrix Hf (x, y) = fxx fxy fyx fyy  is called the Hessian matrix. The sign of the determinant det(Hf ) = D(x, y) = fxx(x, y)fyy (x, y) − �fxy (x, y)2. tells us about its definiteness. At a critical point (a, b): Positive definite: If D(a, b) > 0 and fxx(a, b) > 0, then f has a local minimum. Negative definite: If D(a, b) > 0 and fxx(a, b) < 0, then f has a local maximum. Indefinite: If D(a, b) < 0, then (a, b) is a saddle point. Inconclusive: If D(a, b) = 0, the test is inconclusive. f could have a local max/min, or saddle point at (a, b). 4 / 8

Lagrange multipliers for constrained optimization Suppose we want to optimize f (x, y) subject to the constraint g(x, y) = c. Geometrically, we are searching for the highest or lowest value of f along the constraint curve. At an optimal point on the constraint, the level curve of f is tangent to the constraint curve. That means their normals are parallel: ∇f (x, y) = λ∇g(x, y). Together with the constraint g(x, y) = c, this gives a system of equations to solve. 6 / 8
